Note that if the Sound is a member of a SoundGroup, its playback volume (but not its Volume property) will be influenced by the group's SoundGroup.Volume property.
m.s: The volume of the `Class.Sound`.

kid.simple: How loud the sound is, from 0 (silent) to 10. The default is 0.5.
kid.example:
local sound = workspace:WaitForChild("MySound") -- a Sound in Workspace
sound.Volume = 1 -- twice as loud as the default

m.d: This method pauses playback of the Sound if it is playing, setting Playing to false. Unlike Stop(), it does not reset TimePosition, meaning the sound can be resumed using Resume().
m.s: Pauses playback of the `Class.Sound` if it is playing.

kid.simple: Pauses the sound and remembers where it stopped, so `Resume()` continues from that spot.
kid.example:
local sound = workspace:WaitForChild("MySound") -- a Sound in Workspace
sound:Pause()
task.wait(3)
sound:Resume() -- carries on where it left off

m.dep: This deprecated function is a variant of Sound:Pause() which should be used instead.

kid.simple: Old — use `Sound:Pause` instead (with a capital P).

m.d: This method plays the Sound and sets TimePosition to the last value set by a script (or 0 if it has not been set), then sets Playing to true.
m.s: Plays the `Class.Sound`.

kid.simple: Starts playing the sound. It starts from the time a script last set in `TimePosition`, or from the beginning if none was set.
kid.example:
local sound = workspace:WaitForChild("MySound") -- a Sound in Workspace
sound:Play()
kid.gotcha: If the sound has not loaded yet, it may start late or not be heard. Check `IsLoaded`.

m.dep: This deprecated function is a variant of Sound:Play() which should be used instead.

kid.simple: Old — use `Sound:Play` instead (with a capital P).

m.d: This method resumes the Sound and sets Playing to true. Does not alter TimePosition and thus can be used to resume playback of a sound paused through Pause().
m.s: Resumes the `Class.Sound`.

kid.simple: Continues a paused sound from where it stopped.
kid.example:
local sound = workspace:WaitForChild("MySound") -- a Sound in Workspace
sound:Resume()

m.d: This method stops the Sound and sets Playing to false, then sets TimePosition to 0.
m.s: Stops the `Class.Sound`.

kid.simple: Stops the sound and rewinds it to the beginning (TimePosition goes back to 0).
kid.example:
local sound = workspace:WaitForChild("MySound") -- a Sound in Workspace
sound:Stop()

m.dep: This deprecated function is a variant of Sound:Stop() which should be used instead.

kid.simple: Old — use `Sound:Stop` instead (with a capital S).

m.d:
Fires whenever the Sound loops. Returns soundId and numOfTimesLooped, giving the content ID of the sound and the number of times looped respectively.

When the Sound is stopped through Stop(), the looped counter resets meaning the next DidLoop event will return 1 for numOfTimesLooped.
m.s: Fires whenever the `Class.Sound` loops.

p.s: The SoundId of the Sound that looped.
The number of times the Sound has looped.

kid.simple: Fires every time a looped sound reaches the end and starts again. Tells you the SoundId and how many times it has looped.
kid.example:
local sound = workspace:WaitForChild("MySound") -- a Sound in Workspace
sound.DidLoop:Connect(function(soundId, timesLooped)
    print("Looped", timesLooped, "times")
end)

m.d:
Fires when the Sound has completed playback and stopped. This event is often used to destroy a sound when it has completed playback:

sound:Play()
sound.Ended:Wait()
sound:Destroy()

Note that this event will not fire for sounds with Looped set to true, as they continue playing upon reaching their end. This event will also not fire when the sound is stopped before playback has completed; for this use the Stopped event.
m.s: Fires when the `Class.Sound` has completed playback and stopped.

p.s: The SoundId of the Sound that has ended.

kid.simple: Fires when the sound finishes playing all the way to the end. Often used to delete a sound once it is done.
kid.example:
local sound = workspace:WaitForChild("MySound") -- a Sound in Workspace
sound:Play()
sound.Ended:Wait()
sound:Destroy() -- clean up when done
kid.gotcha: Does not fire for looped sounds, or when you call `Stop()` early.

m.d:
Fires when the Sound is loaded.

As this event only fires at the time the sound is loaded, it's recommended to check the sound's IsLoaded property prior to connecting to this event.
m.s: Fires when the `Class.Sound` is loaded.

p.s: The SoundId of the Sound that loaded.

kid.simple: Fires when the sound has finished loading. Check `IsLoaded` first, because if it already loaded, this event will not fire again.
kid.example:
local sound = workspace:WaitForChild("MySound") -- a Sound in Workspace
if not sound.IsLoaded then
    sound.Loaded:Wait()
end
print("Ready!")

m.d: Fires whenever the Sound is paused using Pause().
m.s: Fires whenever the `Class.Sound` is paused using `Class.Sound:Pause()|Pause()`.

p.s: The SoundId of the Sound that was paused.

kid.simple: Fires when the sound is paused with `Pause()`.
kid.example:
local sound = workspace:WaitForChild("MySound") -- a Sound in Workspace
sound.Paused:Connect(function(soundId)
    print("Paused")
end)

m.d: Fires whenever the Sound is played using Play(). This event will not fire if the Sound is played due to PlayOnRemove being set to true and the sound being destroyed.
m.s: Fires whenever the `Class.Sound` is played using `Class.Sound:Play()|Play()`.

p.s: The SoundId of the Sound that was played.

kid.simple: Fires when the sound is started with `Play()`.
kid.example:
local sound = workspace:WaitForChild("MySound") -- a Sound in Workspace
sound.Played:Connect(function(soundId)
    print("Started playing")
end)

m.d: Fires when the Sound is resumed using Resume().
m.s: Fires when the `Class.Sound` is resumed using `Class.Sound:Resume()|Resume()`.

p.s: The SoundId of the Sound being resumed.

kid.simple: Fires when the sound is continued with `Resume()`.
kid.example:
local sound = workspace:WaitForChild("MySound") -- a Sound in Workspace
sound.Resumed:Connect(function(soundId)
    print("Resumed")
end)

m.d: Fires when the Sound is stopped through using Stop(). Destroying a sound while it is playing will not cause this event to fire.
m.s: Fires when the `Class.Sound` is stopped through using `Class.Sound:Stop()|Stop()`.

p.s: The SoundId of the Sound that stopped.

kid.simple: Fires when the sound is stopped with `Stop()`. Destroying a playing sound does not fire it.
kid.example:
local sound = workspace:WaitForChild("MySound") -- a Sound in Workspace
sound.Stopped:Connect(function(soundId)
    print("Stopped")
end)

kid.simple: A Sound object plays audio, like music, a jump noise or an explosion. You set its SoundId to choose which audio file, then call `:Play()`. If you put it inside a part, the sound comes FROM that part and gets quieter as you walk away. If you put it somewhere else (like Workspace or SoundService), everyone hears it at the same volume everywhere.
kid.analogy: A Sound is like a speaker you can place in the world. Glue it to a part and it is a speaker on that part: louder up close, quieter far away. Leave it unattached and it is like the music playing in your headphones: the same everywhere.
whenToUse: Play background music (put it in Workspace or SoundService and set `Looped = true`)
Play a sound effect from an object, like a ticking clock or a crackling fire (put it inside the part)
Make a noise when something happens, like collecting a coin
Change how fast, loud or long a sound plays
kid.where: Server and client. Create it with Instance.new("Sound") or add one in the Explorer. A sound started by the server is heard by everyone. A sound started by a LocalScript is only heard by that one player (unless SoundService.RespectFilteringEnabled is turned off).

terms.SoundId: The ID of the audio file, written like `rbxassetid://1234567890`. You find audio IDs in the Creator Store or your own uploads.
terms.asset: A file uploaded to Roblox, like an audio clip, image or model. Each has a number ID.
terms.global sound: A sound NOT inside a part or attachment. It plays at the same volume for the player wherever they are.
terms.3D sound (positional sound): A sound inside a part or attachment. It comes from that spot, so it is louder when you are close and comes from the left or right depending on where it is.
terms.listener: The "ears" in the game. By default this is the camera, so sounds are as loud as they would be at the camera's spot.
terms.roll off / attenuate: When a 3D sound gets quieter as you move away from it.
terms.stud: Roblox's unit of length. A default character is about 5 studs tall.
terms.Doppler effect: When a moving sound changes pitch, like a race car sounding higher as it zooms toward you and lower as it zooms away.
terms.pitch: How high or low a sound is. A mouse squeak is high pitch; a lion roar is low pitch.
terms.NumberRange: Two numbers, a Min and a Max, like `NumberRange.new(2, 5)` meaning from 2 to 5.
terms.SoundGroup: A folder-like group of sounds that share a volume and effects. Turn down the "Music" group and every song in it gets quieter.
terms.replicate: To be copied automatically from the server to every player's device.

examples.title: Background music that loops
examples.code:
local SoundService = game:GetService("SoundService")

local music = Instance.new("Sound")
music.SoundId = "rbxassetid://1234567890" -- replace with your music's ID
music.Looped = true   -- start again when it ends
music.Volume = 0.3    -- 0 is silent, 0.5 is the default, 10 is the max
music.Parent = SoundService -- not in a part, so everyone hears it everywhere
music:Play()
explain: We make a new Sound and pick which audio with `SoundId`.
`Looped = true` makes it repeat forever.
Because it is not inside a part, it is a global sound: same volume wherever the player is.
Because a server Script played it, every player hears it.

examples.title: A beep that comes from a part
examples.code:
local part = script.Parent

local beep = Instance.new("Sound")
beep.SoundId = "rbxassetid://9120386436"  -- a horn sound
beep.RollOffMaxDistance = 60  -- can't be heard more than 60 studs away
beep.Parent = part            -- inside the part: it comes from the part

while true do
    beep:Play()
    beep.Ended:Wait() -- wait until it finishes
    task.wait(2)       -- then 2 seconds of quiet
end
explain: Putting the Sound inside a part makes it a 3D sound: walk closer and it gets louder.
`RollOffMaxDistance = 60` means players more than 60 studs away hear nothing.
`beep.Ended:Wait()` pauses the loop until the sound has finished playing.

examples.title: Play a coin sound only for the player who touched it
examples.place: LocalScript in StarterPlayerScripts (needs a Part named Coin with a Sound named Ding inside it)
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local SoundService = game:GetService("SoundService")

local player = Players.LocalPlayer
local coin = workspace:WaitForChild("Coin")
local ding = coin:WaitForChild("Ding")

coin.Touched:Connect(function(otherPart)
    -- only react when MY character touches it
    if otherPart.Parent == player.Character then
        SoundService:PlayLocalSound(ding) -- only I hear it
    end
end)
explain: This runs in a LocalScript, so each player has their own copy.
We check that the part that touched the coin belongs to this player's character.
`PlayLocalSound` plays a copy of the sound that only this player hears.

gotchas: A sound will not play until it has loaded. For important sounds, check `IsLoaded` or wait for `Loaded` first.
A sound inside a part is quieter the further away you are. If you cannot hear it, check `RollOffMaxDistance` and where your camera is.
`Ended` does not fire for looped sounds, and it does not fire when you call `Stop()`; use `Stopped` for that.
`Stop()` rewinds to the start; `Pause()` keeps your place so `Resume()` continues.
Sounds started by a LocalScript are only heard by that player.
Use `PlaybackSpeed` (not the old `Pitch`), and `RollOffMinDistance`/`RollOffMaxDistance` (not `MinDistance`/`MaxDistance`/`EmitterSize`).

class/SoundEffect.d: SoundEffect is the base class that all other sound effects derive from. A SoundEffect can be applied to either a Sound or SoundGroup by being parented to either. Multiple effects can be applied to the same Sound or SoundGroup. The order the effects will be applied in is determined by that effect's Priority.
class/SoundEffect.s: SoundEffect is the base class that all other sound effects derive from. A SoundEffect can be applied to either a `Class.Sound` or `Class.SoundGroup` by being parented to either.

m.d: Toggles the effect on and off. True by default.
m.s: Toggles the effect on and off.

m.d: Determines the order the effect will be applied in relation to other effects. Higher priority effects will be applied earlier. The exception is when Priority equals 0 (which is the default). In this case, the base priority for the effect will be used. If the priority of two effects are equal, then the order is undetermined.
m.s: Determines the order the effect will be applied in relation to other effects.

class/SoundGroup.d:
A SoundGroup is used to manage the volume and effects on multiple Sounds at once. Every sound in the sound group will have its volume adjusted by the group's Volume property which acts as a multiplier, meaning a Sound with volume 0.5 assigned to a SoundGroup with a volume of 0.5 will have an effective volume of 0.25.

If the SoundGroup has any SoundEffects as children, those effects will be applied to all of the Sounds in the group.

Note that a Sound must be added to a SoundGroup by setting its SoundGroup property, not by simply parenting the Sound to the SoundGroup. A Sound can only belong to one SoundGroup at a time, although you can nest groups as outlined here.

See Sound Groups for further details on working with the SoundGroup class.
class/SoundGroup.s: A `Class.SoundGroup` is used to manage the volume and sound effects on multiple `Class.Sound|Sounds` at once. `Class.Sound|Sounds` in the SoundGroup will have their volume and effects adjusted by the SoundGroup.

m.d: The volume multiplier applied to Sounds which belong to the SoundGroup. Value can range from 0 to 10.
m.s: The volume multiplier applied to `Class.Sound|Sounds` that are in the `Class.SoundGroup`.

class/SoundService.d:
A service that determines various aspects of how the audio engine works. Most of its properties affect how Sounds play in the experience, while others affect the behavior of instances in the advanced audio system such as AudioPlayers and AudioEmitters.

SoundService is also often used to store SoundGroups, although this is not mandatory for groups to work.
class/SoundService.s: A service that determines various aspects of how the audio engine works. Most of its properties affect how `Class.Sound|Sounds` play in the experience.

m.d:
Determines at a global level whether sound from AudioEmitters and AudioListeners should automatically implement features of acoustic simulation, such as occlusion (being muffled through walls), diffraction (bending around corners), and reverberation (echoing off of walls).

If set to false, these instances will not simulate these features, regardless of their individual AcousticSimulationEnabled settings.
m.s: Determines whether acoustic simulation is enabled globally in the advanced audio system.

kid.simple: Turns on realistic sound effects for the newer audio system (AudioEmitters and AudioListeners): muffled sound through walls, sound bending around corners, and echoes off walls. If false, these are off everywhere.
kid.example:
local SoundService = game:GetService("SoundService")
SoundService.AcousticSimulationEnabled = true

m.d:
A reverb preset that should be applied to all Sounds in the experience.

Each ReverbType option for this property corresponds to a preset available in the FMOD sound engine. For example, when AmbientReverb is set to ReverbType.Hangar, Sounds will have reverb applied to simulate being in a large enclosed space.

Note that this only affects Sounds and not instances in the advanced audio system such as AudioPlayers and AudioEmitters. See AudioReverb for a way to apply reverb in that system.
m.s: The ambient sound environment preset applied to all `Class.Sound|Sounds`.

kid.simple: Adds an echo style to every Sound in the game, like `Cave`, `Hangar`, `Bathroom` or `NoReverb`.
kid.example:
local SoundService = game:GetService("SoundService")
SoundService.AmbientReverb = Enum.ReverbType.Hangar -- big empty hall echo

m.d: Determines which set of instances core scripts will use to create default character sounds. If set to RolloutState.Enabled, it will use instances in the advanced audio system such as AudioPlayers and AudioEmitters. If set to RolloutState.Disabled, it will use instances in the legacy sound system such as Sounds.
m.s: Determines whether the default character sounds will use instances in the advanced audio system vs. `Class.Sound|Sounds`.

kid.simple: Chooses whether the built-in character sounds (footsteps, jumping and so on) use the newer audio objects or the older Sound objects. Only changeable in Studio's Properties window, not from game scripts.
kid.example:
local SoundService = game:GetService("SoundService")
print(SoundService.CharacterSoundsUseNewApi) -- read-only for game scripts

m.d:
Determines where to place an AudioListener by default. The AudioListener will automatically be wired to a AudioDeviceOutput and will have an empty AudioListener.InteractionGroup set.

See ListenerLocation for detailed descriptions of each option.
m.s: Determines where (if anywhere) to place an `Class.AudioListener` by default.

kid.simple: A Studio setting for where Roblox places the newer AudioListener (the "ears") by default. Normal game scripts cannot read or change it; set it in the Properties window.

m.d:
The number of studs to be considered a meter by SoundService when simulating the Doppler effect for Sounds. This impacts any Sound parented to a BasePart or Attachment.

By default, this property is 3.33, meaning that a meter is considered 3.33 studs for the purposes of simulating the Doppler effect. The greater the DistanceFactor, the faster the listener has to travel relative to Sounds in order to experience the same Doppler shift.

It's recommended that you only change this property if the objects in your experience are scaled differently from what they represent. For example, if your character is meant to be very small (but is normal-sized in the engine), you may want to increase SoundService.DistanceFactor.

Note that this does not impact the behavior of instances in the advanced audio system, such as AudioPlayer or AudioEmitter.
m.s: The number of studs to be considered a meter by `Class.SoundService` when simulating the Doppler effect for `Class.Sound|Sounds`.

kid.simple: How many studs count as one meter for the Doppler effect. The default is 3.33. Only change it if your game's objects are a very different size from normal.
kid.example:
local SoundService = game:GetService("SoundService")
SoundService.DistanceFactor = 3.33

m.d:
This property determines the degree to which the pitch of a Sound varies due to the Doppler effect. This impacts any Sound parented to a BasePart or Attachment.

The Doppler effect is a phenomenon whereby the pitch of a sound changes as the source and observer of the sound move further away or closer together, which is stronger the more quickly they are moving. Increasing SoundService.DopplerScale exaggerates the impact of this effect, whereas decreasing it minimizes it. By default, the value of this property is 1.

Note that this does not impact the behavior of instances in the advanced audio system, such as AudioPlayer or AudioEmitter.
m.s: Degree to which the pitch of a `Class.Sound` varies due to the Doppler effect.

kid.simple: How strong the Doppler effect is (pitch changing when sounds move toward or away from you). 1 is normal, 0 turns it off, bigger numbers exaggerate it.
kid.example:
local SoundService = game:GetService("SoundService")
SoundService.DopplerScale = 0 -- no pitch change from movement

m.d: This property is only functional when ListenerType is set to ListenerType.CFrame. In that scenario, this property determines the world space position from which 3D Sounds are heard by the player.
m.s: The `Datatype.CFrame` that is used as the listener's position if `Class.SoundService.ListenerType|ListenerType` is set to `Enum.ListenerType.CFrame`.

kid.simple: When `ListenerType` is set to CFrame, this is the exact spot and direction the player hears 3D sounds from.
kid.example:
local SoundService = game:GetService("SoundService")
SoundService:SetListener(Enum.ListenerType.CFrame, CFrame.new(0, 10, 0))
print(SoundService.ListenerCFrame)

m.d: This property is only functional when ListenerType is set to ListenerType.ObjectPosition or ListenerType.ObjectCFrame. In that scenario, this property determines which Instance will be used to determine the position from which 3D Sounds are heard by the player. This property can only be set to Instances with a position, such as a BasePart or an Attachment. If it is set to nil, 3D Sounds will not be heard by the player.
m.s: The `Class.Instance` whose translation or coordinate frame is used as the listener's position if `Class.SoundService.ListenerType|ListenerType` is set to `Enum.ListenerType.ObjectPosition` or `Enum.ListenerType.ObjectCFrame`.

kid.simple: When `ListenerType` is ObjectPosition or ObjectCFrame, this is the object (like a part) whose position is used as the player's ears.
kid.example:
local SoundService = game:GetService("SoundService")
print(SoundService.ListenerObject)

m.d:
The listener type for any 3D Sounds in the experience, effectively the point from which 3D Sound audio in the experience is heard by the player. For Sounds parented to a BasePart or Attachment, the listener influences the volume and left/right balance of a playing sound. By default, this listener is set to Workspace.CurrentCamera.

Note that this does not affect the listener location when using the advanced audio system; see AudioListener for a way to set the listener location within that system.

This property may not yet be enabled for all creators. Until full rollout, use SoundService:GetListener() and SoundService:SetListener() instead.
m.s: The current listener type used by 3D `Class.Sound|Sounds` to determine where they will be heard from.

kid.simple: Where the player's ears are for 3D sounds: the `Camera` (default), a fixed `CFrame`, or an object (`ObjectPosition` / `ObjectCFrame`). Change it with `SetListener`.
kid.example:
local SoundService = game:GetService("SoundService")
print(SoundService.ListenerType) -- Enum.ListenerType.Camera

m.d:
This property determines whether Sound playback is replicated from the client to the server, and therefore from the server. In other words, when a LocalScript calls Play() and this property is true, the sound will only play on the respective client. If this property is false, other clients will also hear the sound.

Default is true, meaning filtering is enabled.
m.s: Sets whether `Class.Sound` playback from a client will replicate to the server.

kid.simple: If true (the default), a sound played by a LocalScript is only heard by that player. If false, other players hear it too.
kid.example:
local SoundService = game:GetService("SoundService")
print(SoundService.RespectFilteringEnabled) -- true

m.d:
Determines how fast the volume of a spatialized Sound attenuates. This impacts any Sound parented to a BasePart or Attachment.

A higher RolloffScale means the volume of a Sound will attenuate more rapidly as the distance between the listener and the Sound grows. More precisely, the volume of the Sound will still start attenuating at a distance equal to Sound.RollOffMinDistance, but the attenuation curve will be steeper or more gradual based on the value of RolloffScale. Note that the Sound will still be inaudible past its the Sound.RollOffMaxDistance regardless of the value of SoundService.RolloffScale.

Note that this property does not affect the behavior of instances in the advanced audio system, such as AudioEmitter. See AudioEmitter:SetDistanceAttenuation for a way to apply custom attenuation in that system.
m.s: Determines how fast the volume of a `Class.Sound` attenuates beyond its `Class.Sound.RollOffMinDistance`.

kid.simple: How quickly 3D sounds get quieter with distance, for every Sound. Bigger numbers fade faster; smaller numbers carry further. 1 is normal.
kid.example:
local SoundService = game:GetService("SoundService")
SoundService.RolloffScale = 0.5 -- sounds carry further

m.d:
Determines whether any Sounds parented to a Part emit volumetrically. If set to VolumetricAudio.Enabled, the Sound will simulate being emitted from every point in the interior of the Part. If set to VolumetricAudio.Disabled, the Sound will only emit from a single point in the center of the Part.

Note that this does not impact Sounds parented to other objects, such as Attachments or MeshParts. This also does not impact the behavior of instances in the advanced audio system such as AudioEmitter.
m.s: Determines whether certain spatialized `Class.Sound|Sounds` emit volumetrically, throughout the space of their parent object.

kid.simple: A Studio-only setting: makes a sound inside a Part seem to come from the whole part instead of just its center. Scripts cannot change it; use the Properties window.

m.d:
Returns the current listener type used by Sounds and what object or position that listener is currently set to. This is the point from which Sound audio in the experience is heard by the player. By default, the listener is set to Workspace.CurrentCamera. The listener can be changed using SetListener().

Note that this does not affect the listener location when using the advanced audio system. See AudioListener for a way to set the listener location in that system.
m.s: Returns the current listener type used by `Class.Sound|Sounds`, as well as what that listener is currently set to.

r.s:
A table containing two results. The first result is the listener's ListenerType and the second result is dependent on that type:

Listener Type Description
Enum.ListenerType.Camera Does not return a listener object as Class.Workspace.CurrentCamera|CurrentCamera is always used.
Enum.ListenerType.CFrame Returns the Datatype.CFrame used in Class.SoundService:SetListener()|SetListener().
Enum.ListenerType.ObjectPosition Returns the Class.BasePart used in Class.SoundService:SetListener()|SetListener().
Enum.ListenerType.ObjectCFrame Returns the Class.BasePart used in Class.SoundService:SetListener()|SetListener().

kid.simple: Tells you where the player's ears are: it returns two things, the listener type and the object or CFrame it uses.
kid.example:
local SoundService = game:GetService("SoundService")
local listenerType, listener = SoundService:GetListener()
print(listenerType, listener)

m.d:
Returns a number in seconds that increases as the audio engine produces output. Because this clock is derived from the number of audio samples the mixer has processed, it is stable, sample-accurate, and monotonically increasing, which makes it suitable for scheduling audible changes at precise moments.

Use this value as the basis for the atTime argument of methods that support scheduling playback to begin or end at an exact point in the future, such as Play() and Stop(). Those methods expect times derived from GetMixerTime().

Note, GetMixerTime() starts at an arbitrary value, and can differ between machines. It is not suitable for synchronizing audio across sessions or networks.
m.s: Returns a number in seconds which increases as the audio engine mixes.

r.s: A number in seconds. This value is stable, sample-accurate, and monotonically-increasing. It's intended to be used for scheduling audible changes at precise times.

kid.simple: Gives a very precise audio clock, in seconds, that keeps counting up as audio plays. Use it to start or stop newer AudioPlayers at an exact moment, for music timing.
kid.example:
local SoundService = game:GetService("SoundService")
local player = workspace:WaitForChild("AudioPlayer") -- an AudioPlayer object
player:Play(SoundService:GetMixerTime() + 1) -- start exactly 1 second from now

m.d: Opens the attenuation curve editor in Studio for the provided AudioEmitter or AudioListener instances.
m.s: Opens the attenuation curve editor in Studio for the provided `Class.AudioEmitter` or `Class.AudioListener` instances.

p.s: A list of AudioEmitters or AudioListeners.

kid.simple: For Studio plugins only: opens the editor for how AudioEmitters and AudioListeners fade with distance. Not usable in games.

m.d: Opens the directional curve editor in Studio for the provided AudioEmitter or AudioListener instances. This method is intended for use by Studio plugins that need to programmatically surface the editor, in the same way a user would open it from the Properties window.
m.s: Opens the directional curve editor in Studio for the provided `Class.AudioEmitter` or `Class.AudioListener` instances.

p.s: A list of AudioEmitters or AudioListeners.

kid.simple: For Studio plugins only: opens the editor for how direction changes AudioEmitter and AudioListener volume. Not usable in games.

m.d:
Plays a copy of a Sound locally. The Sound will only be heard by the client calling this method, regardless of where it's parented to.

Some properties of the Sound will be carried over into the copy. These include its Sound.Volume, Sound.TimePosition, Sound.PlaybackSpeed, and any spatialization and effects that are applied to it, including through SoundGroups. Properties that do not affect the copy include Sound.Looped and SoundService.AmbientReverb.
m.s: Plays a copy of a `Class.Sound` locally, such that it will only be heard by the client calling this method.

p.s: The Sound to be played.

kid.simple: Plays a copy of a Sound that only the player running this code hears, no matter where the Sound is. Use it from a LocalScript for menu clicks and personal effects.
kid.example:
local SoundService = game:GetService("SoundService")
-- LocalScript
local ding = SoundService:WaitForChild("Ding") -- a Sound stored in SoundService
SoundService:PlayLocalSound(ding)
kid.gotcha: The copy does not loop even if the original is Looped.

m.d:
Sets the listener type for any Sounds in the experience, which defines the point from which Sound audio in the experience is heard by the player. For Sounds parented to a BasePart or Attachment, the listener influences the volume and left/right balance of a playing sound. By default, this listener is set to Workspace.CurrentCamera.

Note that this does not affect the listener location when using the advanced audio system. See AudioListener for a way to set the listener location in that system.
m.s: Sets the listener used by `Class.Sound|Sounds`.

p.s: The ListenerType of the listener.
Dependent on the ListenerType. Use a BasePart for ListenerType.ObjectPosition or ListenerType.ObjectCFrame, a CFrame for ListenerType.CFrame, or nil for ListenerType.Camera.

kid.simple: Changes where the player's ears are for 3D sounds: the camera, a fixed CFrame, or an object.
kid.example:
local SoundService = game:GetService("SoundService")
-- LocalScript: hear 3D sounds from the character's head instead of the camera
local player = game:GetService("Players").LocalPlayer
local head = (player.Character or player.CharacterAdded:Wait()):WaitForChild("Head")
SoundService:SetListener(Enum.ListenerType.ObjectCFrame, head)

kid.simple: SoundService is the control room for sound in your game. Its settings change how all Sounds behave, like echo, how fast 3D sounds fade with distance, and where the player's "ears" are. It is also a handy place to keep music and SoundGroups, and it can play a sound that only one player hears.
kid.analogy: SoundService is like the sound mixing desk at a concert. It does not sing itself, but it controls the echo, the volume rules, and where the microphones are for everyone.
whenToUse: Play a sound only for one player with `PlayLocalSound` (from a LocalScript)
Add an echo to the whole game, like a cave or big hall, with `AmbientReverb`
Store background music and SoundGroups
Change where the player hears 3D sounds from (the listener)
kid.where: Server and client. Get it with game:GetService("SoundService"). You can also see it in the Explorer and change its settings in the Properties window.

terms.listener: The player's "ears" in the game world. By default it is the camera, so sounds are heard from where the camera is.
terms.reverb: Echo. The way sound bounces off walls, like in a bathroom, cave or gym.
terms.Doppler effect: When a moving sound changes pitch, like a siren sounding higher coming toward you and lower going away.
terms.spatialized (3D) sound: A sound that comes from a place in the world (it is inside a part or attachment), so its volume and left/right side change as you move.
terms.advanced audio system: Roblox's newer set of audio objects (AudioPlayer, AudioEmitter, AudioListener and more) that you wire together. Some SoundService settings only affect these, others only affect the older Sound object.
terms.occlusion: When sound is muffled because a wall is in the way.
terms.replicate: To be copied from one player's device to the server and other players.
terms.filtering: Here, a safety rule that stops a sound played by one player's LocalScript from being heard by everyone.

examples.title: Make the whole game sound like a cave
examples.code:
local SoundService = game:GetService("SoundService")

-- every Sound now has a big echo
SoundService.AmbientReverb = Enum.ReverbType.Cave
explain: `AmbientReverb` adds an echo to every Sound in the game.
Other choices include `Hangar`, `Bathroom`, `Arena` and `NoReverb` (no echo).

examples.title: Click sound only you can hear
examples.place: LocalScript inside a TextButton in StarterGui (with a Sound named Click inside the button)
examples.code:
local SoundService = game:GetService("SoundService")

local button = script.Parent
local click = button:WaitForChild("Click")

button.Activated:Connect(function()
    SoundService:PlayLocalSound(click) -- only this player hears it
end)
explain: `Activated` fires when the player clicks or taps the button.
`PlayLocalSound` plays a copy of the sound just for this player.

gotchas: Several properties (`AmbientReverb`, `DistanceFactor`, `DopplerScale`, `RolloffScale`, `ListenerType`) only affect the older Sound objects, not the newer AudioPlayer/AudioEmitter system.
If `RespectFilteringEnabled` is true (the default), sounds started in a LocalScript are only heard by that player. That is usually what you want.
Setting `ListenerObject` to nil means 3D sounds cannot be heard at all.

class/Sparkles.d:
Sparkles is one of several particle-emitting classes. Like other particle emitters of its kind, Sparkles objects emit particles when parented to a BasePart (such as a Part) or an Attachment within such a BasePart. Compared to the ParticleEmitter class, Sparkles lacks many different customization properties and special methods, such as ParticleEmitter.Lifetime or ParticleEmitter:Emit(). It is useful to create a quick special effect in a pinch; for more detailed work it is preferable to use a ParticleEmitter instead.

When Sparkles.Enabled is toggled off, particles emit by this object will continue to render until their lifetime expires. When a Sparkles object's Instance.Parent is set to nil (and/or Instance:Destroy()ed), all particles will instantly disappear. If this effect is not desired, try hiding the parent object at a far away position, then removing the Sparkles after a few seconds using Debris to give the last particles a chance to expire. This object does not have a ParticleEmitter:Clear() method, but it is possible to set the Instance.Parent to nil and back to the exact same object for the same effect.

Sparkles particles are only emitted from the center of BasePart to which they are parented. Parenting a Sparkles object to an Attachment instead allows customization of the particles' start position.
class/Sparkles.s: A particle emitter with the visual aesthetic of sparkles.

m.d:
The Color property determines the color of all the particles emit by a Sparkles object (both existing and future particles). It behaves similarly to ParticleEmitter.Color, except that it is only one color and not a ColorSequence. Sparkles have a natural color sequence applied which is most apparent when this property is set to white; sparkles very faintly animate between a subtle green and red.

It should be noted that sparkles have a partial ParticleEmitter.LightEmission effect, so dark colors tend to render more transparent and white colors look very bright.
m.s: Determines the color of the sparkle particles.
m.dep: This property is deprecated in favor of Sparkles.SparkleColor, which does the exact same thing.

m.d: The Enabled property, much like ParticleEmitter.Enabled, determines whether sparkle particles are emit. Any particles already emit will continue to render until their lifetime expires. This property is useful for keeping pre-made sparkle effects off until they are needed later. Since sparkle particles are destroyed when the Sparkle object's Instance.Parent is set to nil, this property is useful in allowing existing particles the opportunity to expire before destroying the Fire object altogether. See the function below.
m.s: Determines whether sparkles are emit.

m.d:
This property functions identically to Sparkles.Color.

The SparkleColor property determines the color of all the particles emit by a Sparkles object (both existing and future particles). It behaves similarly to ParticleEmitter.Color, except that it is only one color and not a ColorSequence. Sparkles have a natural color sequence applied which is most apparent when this property is set to white; sparkles very faintly animate between a subtle green and red.

It should be noted that sparkles have a partial ParticleEmitter.LightEmission effect, so dark colors tend to render more transparent and white colors look very bright.
m.s: Determines the color of the sparkle particles.

m.d: A value from 0 to 1 that controls the speed of the sparkle effect. A value of 1 runs the effect at normal speed, 0.5 runs it at half speed, and 0 freezes the effect.
m.s: Controls the speed of the sparkle effect.

class/SpawnLocation.d:
SpawnLocations, or "spawns" determine where a Player respawns when they die. They can be configured to allow only certain players to use each spawn, using Teams. They also control how ForceFields are set up for newly-spawned players.

SpawnLocations can be used as checkpoints, such as in an obstacle course, using the SpawnLocation.AllowTeamChangeOnTouch property, so that when a player touches it, they will change teams to the SpawnLocation's team. In this case, only the first Team should have Team.AutoAssignable set to true, else players will not start at the first checkpoint.

Note if a SpawnLocation is added to the Workspace in Studio with SpawnLocation.Neutral set to false a Team will be created corresponding to SpawnLocation.TeamColor if it does not already exist. This behavior does not occur when spawns are created in-game using a Script or if the properties of the SpawnLocation are changed after already being added. It is recommended that developers always set up their teams manually and not rely on this behavior.

Spawning Rules

There are several rules that come into play for a given SpawnLocation when a player respawns:

  • When SpawnLocation.Neutral is set to false only Players with Player.TeamColor matching SpawnLocation.TeamColor will respawn above it
  • When SpawnLocation.Neutral is set to true any Player can spawn above it regardless of SpawnLocation.TeamColor
  • If multiple eligible spawns are available to a Player, a random one will be chosen
  • Players will spawn at different points on top of a SpawnLocation, but currently, they may still spawn on top of each other if they spawn right after one and other

See also:

  • If you'd like to configure how long it takes for a player to respawn, take a look at the RespawnTime property
class/SpawnLocation.s: `Class.SpawnLocation|SpawnLocations`, or "spawns" determine where a `Class.Player` respawns when they die. They can be configured to allow only certain players to use each spawn, using `Class.Team|Teams`. They also control how `Class.ForceField|ForceFields` are set up for newly-spawned players.

m.d:
Allows a Player to join the team by touching the SpawnLocation. When set to true, if a Player character comes into contact with the SpawnLocation, the player's Player.TeamColor will be set to SpawnLocation.TeamColor. Player.Neutral will also be set to SpawnLocation.Neutral upon contact, meaning a player can also become neutral by touching a spawn location.

This will not function when SpawnLocation.Enabled is set to false.

Making Checkpoints

This feature is often used to make checkpoints in obstacle courses or similar games.
m.s: Allows a `Class.Player` to join the team by touching the `Class.SpawnLocation`. When set to true, if a `Class.Player` character comes into contact with the `Class.SpawnLocation`, the player's `Class.Player.TeamColor` will be set to `Class.SpawnLocation.TeamColor`.

kid.simple: If true, a player who touches this spawn switches to its team (their TeamColor becomes the spawn's TeamColor, and Neutral matches the spawn's Neutral). Used for checkpoints. Does nothing if Enabled is false.
kid.example: spawn.AllowTeamChangeOnTouch = true

m.d:
The length of time, in seconds, that a ForceField will be applied to a Player character spawning at this SpawnLocation. If Duration is zero, the ForceField is never created, and it will not trigger the Instance.DescendantAdded or Instance.ChildAdded events.

This default value of this property is 10 seconds.

The duration feature allows developers to easily give Players protection from 'spawn killing' which can be a frustrating experience for players. Note, ForceFields will only protect users from Explosions and weapons that use Humanoid:TakeDamage() to deal damage or otherwise check for a ForceField.
m.s: The length of time, in seconds, that a `Class.ForceField` will be applied to a `Class.Player` character spawning at this `Class.SpawnLocation`. If Duration is zero, the `Class.ForceField` is never created, and it will not trigger the `Class.Instance.DescendantAdded` or `Class.Instance.ChildAdded` events.

kid.simple: How many seconds the spawn ForceField lasts on players who appear here. Default 10. 0 means no ForceField at all.
kid.example: spawn.Duration = 3 -- short protection

m.d:
Sets whether or not the SpawnLocation is enabled. When disabled players cannot spawn at the SpawnLocation and the SpawnLocation.AllowTeamChangeOnTouch functionality is disabled.

This property provides the most convenient way of preventing Players from spawning at a spawn.

Note, although team changing on touch using SpawnLocation.AllowTeamChangeOnTouch is disabled when Enabled is set to false, other touched events using BasePart.Touched will still fire.
m.s: Sets whether or not the `Class.SpawnLocation` is enabled. When disabled players cannot spawn at the `Class.SpawnLocation` and the AllowTeamChangeOnTouch functionality is disabled.

kid.simple: If false, nobody can spawn here and touching it won't change teams. The easiest way to turn a spawn off.
kid.example: spawn.Enabled = false

m.d:
Whether or not a spawn is affiliated with a specific team. This means that any Player, of any Team, can spawn on it if this property is set to true.

If Neutral is set to false, only players whose Player.TeamColor is equal to SpawnLocation.TeamColor can use the SpawnLocation.

If SpawnLocation.AllowTeamChangeOnTouch is true Player.Neutral will be set to this property upon contact with the spawn.
m.s: Whether or not a `Class.SpawnLocation` is affiliated with a specific team. This means that any `Class.Player`, of any `Class.Team`, can spawn on it if this property is set to true.

kid.simple: If true, any player of any team can spawn here. If false, only players whose TeamColor matches the spawn's TeamColor can.
kid.example: spawn.Neutral = false

m.d:
The TeamColor property sets what team the SpawnLocation is affiliated to. If SpawnLocation.Neutral property is false, only Players with the same Player.TeamColor as the spawn's TeamColor will be able to spawn there.

If SpawnLocation.AllowTeamChangeOnTouch is true Player.Neutral will be set to this property upon contact with the spawn.
m.s: Sets what team the `Class.SpawnLocation` is affiliated to. If `Class.SpawnLocation.Neutral` property is false, only `Class.Player|Players` with the same `Class.Player.TeamColor` as the spawn's TeamColor will be able to spawn there.

kid.simple: Which team this spawn belongs to (by color). Only matters when Neutral is false. Must match the Team's TeamColor.
kid.example: spawn.TeamColor = BrickColor.new("Bright red")

kid.simple: A SpawnLocation is a special part where players appear when they join and after they die. It can be open to everyone or only to one team. It also gives freshly spawned players a short-lived ForceField so nobody can attack them right away.
kid.analogy: A SpawnLocation is like a starting line in a race. Everyone (or every runner on a certain team) lines up there at the start, and again after they're knocked out.
whenToUse: Choose where players appear in your world.
Make different start areas for different teams.
Make obby checkpoints: touch a spawn and you'll respawn there next time.
kid.where: In Workspace. Insert one from the Model tab in Studio, or with `Instance.new("SpawnLocation")`. It is a kind of Part, so it has all the normal Part properties (Size, Color, Anchored...) too.

terms.spawn: Appearing in the world with a new character.
terms.ForceField: The sparkly bubble around a just-spawned player. It blocks explosions and TakeDamage while it lasts.
terms.spawn killing: Attacking players the moment they appear, before they can move. ForceFields help stop it.
terms.neutral: Not tied to any team. A neutral spawn can be used by anyone.
terms.TeamColor: The BrickColor that links a spawn to the Team with the same color.
terms.checkpoint: A save point in an obby. After falling, you start from the last checkpoint instead of the beginning.

examples.title: Team-only spawns
examples.place: Set up in Studio (no script needed)
examples.code:
-- 1. In Teams, add a Team. Name it "Blue Team", set TeamColor to Bright blue.
-- 2. In Workspace, add a SpawnLocation.
-- 3. On the SpawnLocation: untick Neutral, set TeamColor to Bright blue.
-- Now only Blue Team players spawn here.

-- Same setup done by script (Script in ServerScriptService):
local spawn = Instance.new("SpawnLocation")
spawn.Anchored = true
spawn.Size = Vector3.new(6, 1, 6)
spawn.Position = Vector3.new(0, 0.5, 40)
spawn.Neutral = false
spawn.TeamColor = BrickColor.new("Bright blue")
spawn.Parent = workspace
explain: Neutral = false means 'only one team can use this spawn'.
TeamColor must exactly match the Team's TeamColor.
If more than one spawn fits a player, Roblox picks one at random.
SpawnLocation.TeamColor is about which team can use it. The part's BrickColor/Color is just how it looks.

examples.title: Obby checkpoints
examples.place: Studio setup plus a Script in ServerScriptService
examples.code:
-- For each checkpoint: make a Team (e.g. "Stage 1", "Stage 2") with its own TeamColor,
-- and a SpawnLocation with the same TeamColor, Neutral off, and AllowTeamChangeOnTouch on.
-- Only the Stage 1 team should have AutoAssignable on, so new players start there.

-- Optional: a simpler checkpoint without teams, using RespawnLocation
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local checkpoint = workspace:WaitForChild("Checkpoint2") -- a SpawnLocation (Neutral on)

checkpoint.Touched:Connect(function(hit)
    local player = Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(hit.Parent)
    if player then
        player.RespawnLocation = checkpoint -- next respawn happens here
    end
end)
explain: With AllowTeamChangeOnTouch, touching the spawn switches you to its team, so you'll respawn on it next time.
The second way skips teams: Player.RespawnLocation picks which SpawnLocation the player uses next time.
RespawnLocation only works if the spawn is Neutral or matches the player's TeamColor.

gotchas: Set the spawn's Anchored to true, or it may fall or be pushed away.
TeamColor is not the same as the part's visible Color or BrickColor.
If no spawn fits a player (for example all are locked to other teams), they won't spawn where you expect.
ForceFields only stop damage that respects them (explosions and Humanoid:TakeDamage). Setting Health directly ignores them.

class/SpawnerService.d: An internal service that is responsible for the behavior of SpawnLocations. Its functionality is not accessible to developers.
class/SpawnerService.s: An internal service that is responsible for the behavior of `Class.SpawnLocation|SpawnLocations`. Its functionality is not accessible to developers.

class/SpecialMesh.d:
The SpecialMesh object applies a mesh to a BasePart depending on the MeshType property. A number of options are available.

  • Brick - A block shape, equivalent to a BlockMesh
  • Cylinder - A cylinder, identical to a Part with a Part.Shape of 'Cylinder'
  • FileMesh - A user uploaded Mesh, equivalent to FileMesh that a texture can be applied to using the FileMesh.TextureId property
  • Head - A character head shape
  • Sphere - A sphere shape, similar to a Part with a Part.Shape of 'Ball' but can be freely resized on all axis
  • Wedge - A wedge shape, identical to a WedgePart
  • Torso - A block with sloped sides, due to be deprecated

Note, each SpecialMesh.MeshType will scale differently when using DataModelMesh.Scale, for more information on this please see the page on DataModelMesh.Scale. The SpecialMesh object also exposes the DataModelMesh.Offset property.

It is important to remember that when using a SpecialMesh, only the appearance of a part changes. The collision model of the part remains the same. For example, a character will not be able to walk correctly over a mesh as the mesh geometry is not taken into account.

SpecialMesh vs MeshPart

There are currently two ways of using a developer created mesh. They are using a SpecialMesh with the SpecialMesh.FileType set to 'FileMesh', or by using a MeshPart. Although, on the whole, the MeshPart object has superseded the SpecialMesh there are some differences developers should be aware of.

  • BasePart.Material displays correctly on the mesh when using a MeshPart and not when using a SpecialMesh
  • MeshParts include the MeshPart.CollisionFidelity property, meaning the collision model of a MeshPart can be set to resemble the geometry of the mesh. The SpecialMesh object by contrast, uses the parent BaseParts collision model
  • The mesh of a MeshPart scales on all axis depending on the Size property of the MeshPart, the mesh of a SpecialMesh does not
  • The SpecialMesh object includes the Offset and Scale properties whereas MeshParts do not
  • The MeshId property of a SpecialMesh can be changed by a Script or LocalScript during runtime. The MeshId property of a MeshPart can not.
class/SpecialMesh.s: The `Class.SpecialMesh` object applies a mesh to a `Class.BasePart` depending on the `Class.SpecialMesh.MeshType|MeshType` property.

m.d:
The mesh that the SpecialMeshobject applies to the BasePart depends on the MeshType property. A number of options are available.

  • Brick - A block shape, equivalent to a BlockMesh
  • Cylinder - A cylinder, identical to a Part with a Part.Shape of 'Cylinder'
  • FileMesh - A user uploaded Mesh, equivalent to FileMesh that a texture can be applied to using the FileMesh.TextureId property
  • Head - A character head shape
  • Sphere - A sphere shape, similar to a Part with a Part.Shape of 'Ball' but can be freely resized on all axis
  • Wedge - A wedge shape, identical to a WedgePart
  • Torso - A block with sloped sides, due to be deprecated

Note, each MeshType will scale differently when using DataModelMesh.Scale, for more information on this please see the page on DataModelMesh.Scale.
m.s: Determines the type of mesh that will be applied to the `Class.BasePart` the `Class.SpecialMesh` is parented to.

class/SphereHandleAdornment.d: SphereHandleAdornment is a sphere-shaped handle that can be adorned to a BasePart. If parented to a player's PlayerGui or the CoreGui, handles can listen to input events for purposes such as making dragger tools.
class/SphereHandleAdornment.s: A sphere-shaped handle that can be adorned to a `Class.BasePart`.

m.d: The radius of the sphere adornment in studs.
m.s: Radius of the sphere adornment.

m.d:
Shading selects the material and render pass used to draw the sphere, via AdornShading. It defaults to AdornShading.Default, which draws the sphere unlit and occluded by scene geometry like an ordinary world object.

AdornShading.Shaded and AdornShading.XRayShaded light the sphere with the scene's lighting instead of drawing it unlit, while AdornShading.XRay and AdornShading.XRayShaded draw the sphere through geometry that would otherwise occlude it. AdornShading.AlwaysOnTop draws the sphere on top of everything else with no depth testing.

The legacy HandleAdornment.AlwaysOnTop property only takes effect while Shading is AdornShading.Default; any other Shading value determines the render pass on its own.
m.s: Determines how the sphere adornment is shaded and whether it draws through geometry that would otherwise occlude it.

class/SpotLight.d:
A Spotlight emits light of a specified Color and Brightness in the shape of a cone with a spherical base. This object is ideal for directional light sources like flashlights and headlights.

Range controls the distance of illumination and Angle defines the angle of light emission from the cone's apex as illustrated below.

A spotlight must be a direct child of a BasePart or Attachment and will exhibit the following behavior:

  • When the spotlight is parented to a BasePart, the Face property determines the face of the part from which light emanates.

  • Although Attachments don't have faces, the Face property determines the axis of the attachment from which light emanates; -Z is front, +X is right, +Y is top, etc.

See also SurfaceLight and PointLight.
class/SpotLight.s: A light source that emits light directionally in the shape of a cone with a spherical base.

m.d: The angle of which the light is shone from the SpotLight.
m.s: The angle of which the light is shone from the SpotLight.

m.d: Sets the side of the parent that the SpotLight comes from.
m.s: Sets the side of the parent that the SpotLight comes from.

m.d: The size of the area that the SpotLight will illuminate.
m.s: The size of the area that the SpotLight will illuminate.

class/SpringConstraint.d:
A SpringConstraint applies a force to its Attachments based on spring and damper behavior. This constraint, along with a CylindricalConstraint, is ideal for building vehicle suspension.

Note that if this constraint attaches one part (A) to another part (B) that is anchored or connected to an anchored part (Z), part A will not be locally simulated when interacting with a player.

When configuring this constraint, it may be helpful to study Roblox Units to understand how Roblox units compare to metric units.

Free Length

FreeLength defines the natural resting length of the spring. If the attachments are further apart than the free length, they are forced together; if the attachments are closer together than the free length, they are forced apart.

Damping

The Damping value controls how fast the spring's oscillation dies down. A value of 0 allows the spring to oscillate endlessly, while higher values bring the spring to a rest more quickly.

Stiffness

Stiffness sets the strength of the spring. Higher values create a spring that responds with more force when its attachments are closer together or further apart than FreeLength.

Limits

Enabling the LimitsEnabled property exposes the MinLength and MaxLength values for setting the minimum and maximum length of the spring. If the spring's attachments reach these limits, they stop moving apart from one another without restitution.
class/SpringConstraint.s: Simulates spring and damper behavior between two attachments.

m.d: The number of coils visualized on the SpringConstraint. This can only be set between 0 and 8.
m.s: The number of coils visualized on the `Class.SpringConstraint`.

kid.simple: How many coils are drawn (0 to 8). Only changes the look.
kid.example: workspace.Ceiling.SpringConstraint.Coils = 8

m.d: The current distance between the constraint's Attachments.
m.s: The current distance between the constraint's `Class.Attachment|Attachments`.

kid.simple: Read-only: the distance between the two attachments right now, in studs.
kid.example: print(workspace.Ceiling.SpringConstraint.CurrentLength)

m.d: Damping constant for the SpringConstraint. Multiplied to the velocity of the constraint's Attachments to reduce the spring force applied.
m.s: Damping constant for the `Class.SpringConstraint`. Multiplied to the velocity of the constraint's `Class.Attachment|Attachments` to reduce the spring force applied.

kid.simple: How much the spring resists fast movement, which calms bouncing down. It is multiplied by how fast the attachments are moving, so it only matters while they move. 0 = bounces forever.
kid.example: workspace.Car.Spring.Damping = 200

m.d: Natural resting length of the spring.
m.s: Natural resting length of the spring.

kid.simple: The relaxed length of the spring in studs. Longer than this, it pulls in; shorter, it pushes out.
kid.example: workspace.Trampoline.SpringConstraint.FreeLength = 3

m.d: Sets whether the SpringConstraint enforces a minimum and maximum length. If the constraint's Attachments reach these limits, they will simply stop moving apart from one another without restitution. If you need restitution or elasticity at the ends of the range of motion, you can combine a SpringConstraint with another constraint that allows restitution at the end of its range, such as a PrismaticConstraint or RopeConstraint.
m.s: Sets whether the `Class.SpringConstraint` enforces a minimum and maximum length.

kid.simple: If true, the spring can never get shorter than MinLength or longer than MaxLength. It just stops there with no bounce.
kid.example:
local spring = workspace.Car.Spring
spring.LimitsEnabled = true
spring.MinLength = 1
spring.MaxLength = 4
kid.gotcha: For a bouncy stop at the ends, add a RopeConstraint or PrismaticConstraint with Restitution.

m.d: The maximum force the SpringConstraint can apply on its Attachments. Some spring systems can give rise to forces that grow fast leading to instability. In such cases it is recommended to set MaxForce to a reasonable value.
m.s: The maximum force the `Class.SpringConstraint` can apply on its `Class.Attachment|Attachments`.

kid.simple: The most force the spring may push or pull with. Setting a sensible number stops very stiff springs from going wild.
kid.example: workspace.Car.Spring.MaxForce = 50000

m.d: The maximum separation the SpringConstraint will allow if LimitsEnabled is true.
m.s: The maximum separation the SpringConstraint will allow if `Class.SpringConstraint.LimitsEnabled|LimitsEnabled` is true.

kid.simple: The longest the spring may stretch, in studs, when LimitsEnabled is true.
kid.example: workspace.Car.Spring.MaxLength = 5

m.d: The minimum separation the SpringConstraint will allow if LimitsEnabled is true.
m.s: The minimum separation the SpringConstraint will allow if `Class.SpringConstraint.LimitsEnabled|LimitsEnabled` is true.

kid.simple: The shortest the spring may squash, in studs, when LimitsEnabled is true.
kid.example: workspace.Car.Spring.MinLength = 0.5

m.d: The visualized radius of the spring's coils.
m.s: The visualized radius of the spring's coils.

kid.simple: How wide the drawn coils look. Only changes the look.
kid.example: workspace.Car.Spring.Radius = 0.6

m.d: The strength of the spring. The higher this value the more force will be applied when the attachments are separated a different length than the FreeLength.
m.s: The strength of the spring. The higher this value the more force will be applied when the attachments are separated a different length than the `Class.SpringConstraint.FreeLength|FreeLength`.

kid.simple: How strong the spring is. The push or pull is about Stiffness x (how far it is from FreeLength). Stiffness 1000 squashed 2 studs pushes with about 2000.
kid.example:
local spring = workspace.Trampoline.SpringConstraint
spring.Stiffness = 3000 -- a strong, springy trampoline

m.d: The visualized thickness of the spring's coils.
m.s: The visualized thickness of the spring's coils.

kid.simple: How thick the drawn coil wire looks. Only changes the look.
kid.example: workspace.Car.Spring.Thickness = 0.1

kid.simple: SpringConstraint acts like a real spring between two attachments. If they get farther apart than its resting length, it pulls them back together; if they get squashed closer, it pushes them apart. Stiffness says how strong the spring is, and Damping says how fast the bouncing calms down.
kid.analogy: SpringConstraint is like the spring inside a pogo stick or the shock absorbers on a car: squash it and it pushes back, and the damper stops it bouncing forever.
whenToUse: Car and vehicle suspension (often with CylindricalConstraint)
Bouncy trampolines and launch pads
Wobbly, springy decorations
Soft connections that stretch a bit
kid.where: Make it with Instance.new("SpringConstraint"), set Attachment0 and Attachment1 (one in each part) and put it in workspace. Set Visible = true to draw it as a coil.

terms.constraint: An invisible rule or connector that the physics engine follows, like 'these two parts must stay stuck together' or 'push this part upward'.
terms.attachment: A tiny invisible point you put inside a part. It has a position AND a direction (its own X, Y and Z arrows). Constraints grab parts by their attachments.
terms.Attachment0 / Attachment1: The two attachments a constraint connects. Attachment0 is usually the one that gets pushed or moved; Attachment1 is the other end or the goal.
terms.force: A push or pull. In Roblox it is measured in Roblox force units (mass x studs per second per second). A bigger number is a harder push.
terms.mass: How much 'stuff' an object has, which decides how hard it is to push. A part's mass = its volume x its material density. A 4x1x2 Plastic part (volume 8, density 0.7) has mass 5.6.
terms.gravity: The pull that makes things fall. In Roblox it is `workspace.Gravity`, which is 196.2 studs per second per second by default.
terms.velocity: Speed plus direction, written as a Vector3 in studs per second. Vector3.new(0, 0, 20) means 20 studs every second along the Z direction.
terms.stiffness: How strong a spring is. A stiff spring pushes back hard when you squash or stretch it even a little.
terms.damping: Something that slows wobbling down, like shock absorbers in a car. 0 means it bounces forever; bigger numbers settle down faster.
terms.stud: Roblox's unit of length. A default baseplate grid square is 1 stud; a classic character is about 5 studs tall.
terms.anchored: An anchored part is frozen in place. Physics and constraint forces cannot move it. Set `part.Anchored = false` if you want a constraint to move it.
terms.unanchored: A part that physics is allowed to move. Constraints that push or pull only work on unanchored parts.
terms.MaxForce: A cap (upper limit) on how hard a constraint is allowed to push. It is a limit, not the amount it always pushes.
terms.limits: Stops that keep a joint from moving too far, like a door that can only swing 90 degrees.
terms.restitution: Bounciness, from 0 (no bounce, just stops) to 1 (bounces back as hard as it hit).
terms.FreeLength: The spring's relaxed length, when it is neither pushing nor pulling.
terms.oscillate: Bounce back and forth again and again, like a spring toy.
terms.spring force: Roughly Stiffness x (how far from FreeLength). A spring with Stiffness 100 stretched 2 studs too long pulls with about 200 force.
terms.suspension: The springy parts that connect a car's wheels to its body so bumps do not shake it too much.

examples.title: Hang a bouncy block from a spring
examples.code:
local ceiling = workspace:WaitForChild("Ceiling") -- anchored part
local ball = workspace:WaitForChild("Ball")       -- unanchored part

local a0 = Instance.new("Attachment")
a0.Parent = ceiling
local a1 = Instance.new("Attachment")
a1.Parent = ball

local spring = Instance.new("SpringConstraint")
spring.Attachment0 = a0
spring.Attachment1 = a1
spring.FreeLength = 6    -- relaxed length: 6 studs
spring.Stiffness = 500   -- how strong the spring is
spring.Damping = 10      -- calms the bouncing down over time
spring.Visible = true    -- draw the coil
spring.Coils = 6
spring.Parent = ceiling

while true do
	print("Spring length now:", spring.CurrentLength)
	task.wait(0.5)
end
explain: The spring wants to be 6 studs long. Gravity pulls the ball down, stretching it a bit more.

It settles where spring pull = weight. If the ball has mass 5.6, its weight is 5.6 x 196.2 = about 1098.7, so a Stiffness of 500 stretches about 1098.7 / 500 = about 2.2 studs past 6, ending near 8.2 studs.
Damping 10 makes the bouncing fade. With Damping 0 it would bounce forever.
CurrentLength tells you how long the spring is right now.

examples.title: Pick a stiffness for car suspension
examples.code:
local car = workspace:WaitForChild("Car")
local body = car:WaitForChild("Body")

-- Weight of the whole car: mass x gravity
local weight = body.AssemblyMass * workspace.Gravity
-- 4 springs share the weight. We want each one squashed by 1 stud.
local squash = 1
local stiffness = (weight / 4) / squash

for _, spring in car:GetDescendants() do
	if spring:IsA("SpringConstraint") then
		spring.Stiffness = stiffness
		spring.Damping = stiffness / 20 -- a little damping so it does not wobble forever
	end
end
print("Each spring stiffness:", stiffness)
explain: A spring's push is about Stiffness x squash. To hold the car up, the 4 springs together must push with the car's weight.
For a car with mass 100: weight = 100 x 196.2 = 19620. Each spring holds 4905, so for a 1-stud squash, Stiffness = 4905.
The damping amount here is just a starting guess; tune it until the ride feels right.

gotchas: A spring with no Damping bounces forever. Add some damping.
If Stiffness is too low compared to the weight, the spring squashes flat. Use weight (mass x 196.2) to estimate it.
Very stiff springs can go unstable and shake wildly. Set MaxForce to a sensible limit.
Limits (MinLength/MaxLength) stop the spring without any bounce.

If a part is joined this way to an anchored part (or something connected to an anchored part), its physics is not calculated on the player's own device when they touch it, so it may feel slightly delayed.

class/StandalonePluginScripts.d:
StandalonePluginScripts is a container of Scripts to be run in a standalone plugin DataModel when Roblox Studio starts (it is not useful outside the context of plugins). When a place to be edited is loaded in Roblox Studio, scripts inside this container are not run.

Limited Functionality and Availability

Functionality of this class may be enabled or disabled without notice. Before using it, verify that it works as expected before continuing with further work.
class/StandalonePluginScripts.s: A container for `Class.Script|Scripts` that run only in the standalone plugin `Class.DataModel` at Roblox Studio startup.

class/StandardPages.d: A generic version of the Pages class, which may contain variable data, depending on what method it was returned from. See the Pages class for more information.
class/StandardPages.s: A generic Pages object that can contain variable data depending on the method that returned it.

class/StarterCharacterScripts.d:
The StarterCharacterScripts container stores scripts to be parented to a player's Player.Character when it spawns. Unlike scripts stored in the StarterPlayerScripts folder, these scripts will not persist when the character respawns.

If a LocalScript named Animate, Sound, or Health is placed in this container, it will replace the default script that manages character animations, character sounds, and character health regeneration respectively.
class/StarterCharacterScripts.s: Stores instances to be parented to a player's character when it spawns.

class/StarterGear.d:
When a player spawns, the contents of that player's StarterGear is copied into the player's Backpack. Additionally, if the game allows gear, all of the appropriate gear Tools that the player owns are inserted into that player's StarterGear.

Unlike StarterPack, StarterGear isn't a service but rather a child of each Player object, so its contents are player‑specific. Whether or not gear can be permitted is determined in a place's Permissions settings. You can enable gear by its genre or choose specific types to allow. To disable gear, ensure all the gear types are unselected.

Listening to the Players.PlayerAdded event from a server Script is useful for accessing StarterGear:

local Players = game:GetService("Players")

local toolPrefab = Instance.new("Tool")
toolPrefab.Name = "Example Tool"

local function onPlayerAdded(player)
    -- Wait for StarterGear to be added
    local starterGear = player:WaitForChild("StarterGear")
    -- Clone prefab tool to StarterGear
    local toolClone = toolPrefab:Clone()
    toolClone.Parent = starterGear
end

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(onPlayerAdded)

Gameplay Considerations

Always test experiences after adding gear to them to check that users can't easily abuse them there. Gear may include Script objects which allow the player to perform actions that you might not consider; for example, navigational gear might allow the player to access a part of the map that you don't want them to, and weapon gear may allow the holder to damage other players, possibly without retribution or retaliation.
class/StarterGear.s: If the game allows gear, `StarterGear` is a container automatically inserted into each `Class.Player` object when the player joins the game. Whenever the player's character spawns, the contents of that player's `StarterGear` are copied into the player's `Class.Backpack`.

class/StarterGui.d:
StarterGui is a container object designed to hold LayerCollector objects such as ScreenGuis.

When a Player.Character spawns, the contents of their PlayerGui (if any) are emptied. Children of the StarterGui are then copied along with their descendants into the PlayerGui. Note, however, that LayerCollector objects such as ScreenGuis with their ResetOnSpawn property set to false will only be placed into each player's PlayerGui once and will not be deleted when the Player respawns.

StarterGui also includes a range of functions allowing you to interact with the CoreGui. For example StarterGui:SetCoreGuiEnabled() can be used to disable elements of the CoreGui, and StarterGui:SetCore() can perform a range of functions including creating notifications and system messages.
class/StarterGui.s: A container for `Class.LayerCollector` objects to be copied into the `Class.PlayerGui` of `Class.Player|Players`. Also provides a range of functions for interacting with the `Class.CoreGui`.
